assumptions.name: Net flows

market.note: UK advice peers average 2.4% net flows

competitive.note: Reported net flows negative in each of the last three years

track_record.note: No period of sustained positive flows since acquisitions began

assumptions.rationale: Gross inflows rise 6.5% to 11% of AuA with withdrawals held at 5–6%, on a client base averaging 67. Reported net flows were negative in each of the last three years; UK advice peers average 2.4%.

sensitivity.comment: Impacts the yearly inflow rate; £130m less AuA by 2030

deep_dive.headline: 1. [Target]'s AuA growth plan seems realistic, with potential market upside offsetting an optimistic net-flow recovery

panels.title: 1a. Net flows
body: The assumed turnaround lacks sufficient historical support. Net flows have historically lagged sector peers, which management attributes to disruption from M&A integration.
Reaching 2.5% by 2030 requires a sustained improvement while the business continues to pursue an ambitious acquisition programme.

panels.title: 1b. Market movement
body: The assumed 3.0% annual market growth provides potential upside. The forecast tracks inflation and sits below the returns historically delivered by the client portfolios.
Continued investment performance could offset weaker-than-planned net flows.
panels.chart_title: Projected net flows and market movement, % of AuA

assessment.title: AuA evolution assessment
bullets: The combined AuA trajectory appears achievable, although its principal buffer lies outside management's control.
Conservative market-growth assumptions balance the optimistic net-flow forecast, leaving delivery more dependent on market performance than on demonstrated organic-flow execution.

deep_dive.source: Factset; [Target] CIM; vendor CDD; Aqmen analysis

assumptions.name: Market movement

market.note: Balanced portfolios delivered ~4.4% net over five years

competitive.note: In line with peers' planning assumptions

track_record.note: Client portfolios have tracked market benchmarks

assumptions.rationale: 3.0% a year net of a 1.3% fee drag, equal to plan inflation, so zero real return for five years. A balanced risk profile has delivered ~4.4% net over the last five years.

sensitivity.comment: Impacts the yearly return on the book; £202m less AuA by 2030

assumptions.name: Lead generation
assumptions.rationale: Lead conversion nearly doubles and new clients rise from 740 to 1,500 a year, against ~1% conversion to date and under two years of track record.

sensitivity.comment: Fewer leads with conversion and client size held constant; £69m less AuA by 2030

assumptions.name: Adviser recruitment

market.note: 288 hires is <10% of the ~3,000-adviser core priority pool

competitive.note: 13 of 16 appointments to date came from one competitor

track_record.note: Historical hiring ~22 a year; plan needs ~63 from 2027

assumptions.rationale: Hiring at 2.9× the historical 22 a year, full retention of every hire against 59% historically, and no attrition on the existing adviser base against 20% a year. Three gaps, each material on its own.

sensitivity.comment: Fewer advisers hired with AuA and productivity per adviser held constant; £503m less AuA by 2030

deep_dive.headline: 2. Recruitment plan deemed highly optimistic as it needs 2.9× the historical hiring rate and a shift from 59% to 100% retention

panels.title: Gross adviser hiring evolution
body: Annualising the 2026 recruitment run rate implies 24 hires, 12 fewer than assumed in the business plan.
panels.chart_title: Gross adviser hires per year, historical and plan

assessment.title: Recruitment assessment
bullets: **Throughput has no precedent at this level.** The channel delivered ~22 advisers a year over 2023 to 2025; the plan averages ~63 from 2027, a 2.9× step-up.
**The current initiative is behind its own first year.** Six months into FY26, 11 of the 36 planned hires had been inducted.
**Zero churn is the harder assumption.** 41% of advisers recruited FY23 to Jan-26 were not retained; the model has no attrition input.
**Supply is not the constraint.** 288 hires is under 10% of the core pool, but requires capturing ~10% of the addressable outflow from a ~1% market share.

deep_dive.source: Vendor CDD; [Target] business plan (adviser recruitment assumptions); Aqmen analysis

assumptions.name: Platform

track_record.note: Penetration fell every year since FY23 (53% to 48%)

assumptions.rationale: Penetration rises 2pp a year after falling every year since FY23, requiring acquired books to migrate at a pace not yet demonstrated.

sensitivity.comment: 10% less migrated onto the platform; applies to all growth channels

assumptions.name: Funds

competitive.note: Fund pricing below peers supports adoption

track_record.note: FY25 onboards are 53% in own funds

assumptions.rationale: In line with recent cohorts: FY25 onboards are 53% in own funds and the pre-FY23 book is above 50%. Assumes those levels hold and the legacy book does not drift.

sensitivity.comment: 10% less migrated into own funds; applies to all growth channels

assumptions.name: Advisory fee

market.note: Regulatory and AI pressure on advice pricing beyond FY28

assumptions.rationale: In line with historical yields, held at 88–91bps since FY23. [Target] is among the lowest-priced peers, so it keeps its price for three years; uncertainty thereafter from the FCA ongoing-advice review and AI-enabled advice.

sensitivity.comment: Lower price on every pound advised in all growth channels; £20.4m less revenue in 2030

deep_dive.headline: 4. [Target]'s advisory fee appears defensible through FY28, with increasing uncertainty thereafter

panels.title: UK advice tariffs
body: [Target] charges 80 to 100bps for financial planning plus its model portfolios, 93bps weighted across its book. Benchmarked peers charge 99 to 127bps for the same bundle.
Of the peers with disclosed history, none has cut its ongoing advice tariff.
panels.chart_title: Bundled planning and investment management tariff, bps, 2025

panels.title: What [Target] earns
body: The core book has earned 88 to 91bps every year since FY23, about 96% of its 93bps weighted tariff.
The blended figure fell from 96 to 88bps as £3m of ongoing fees from legacy acquired clients ran off when those clients migrated or exited under Consumer Duty. It is not a price cut.
panels.chart_title: Realised ongoing advice charge, bps of average AuA

assessment.title: Advisory fee assessment
bullets: [Target] already charges less than UK peers for the same bundle, so it is not the obvious first target for repricing.
Its own history shows no compression; expert input describes flat advice pricing as defensible for two to three years, with fund fees under pressure first.
Beyond FY28 two open questions remain: the FCA's ongoing-advice review and whether AI-enabled advice resets the price point.

deep_dive.source: [Target] business plan model; vendor CDD; peer annual reports; Aqmen expert interviews

assumptions.name: Platform fee

market.note: Expert view: platform is the last fee to move, to 10–15bps beyond the horizon

assumptions.rationale: In line with the FY25 actual of 19.8bps and confirmed by the trading DD. Expert view is that platform is the last fee to move, drifting to 10–15bps beyond the plan horizon.

sensitivity.comment: Lower price on the book held on platform; £2.1m less revenue in 2030

assumptions.name: Fund fee

market.note: Passive cores at 10–25bps and fair-value reviews press fund fees

competitive.note: In line with vertically integrated peers

track_record.note: 48bps achieved in two months after a fund launch; 45bps in FY23–FY25

assumptions.rationale: Assumes the 48bps achieved in the two months after the latest fund launch is the new run rate, versus 45bps in FY23–FY25. Fund fees face the most downward pressure, from passive cores at 10–25bps and fair-value reviews.

sensitivity.comment: Lower price on the book held in own funds; £5.0m less revenue in 2030
